title: EUDR reference-number desk for downstream buyers
one_liner: An inbox-and-validator service that collects, checks and vaults EUDR reference numbers and plot GeoJSON from suppliers, sold to downstream operators and via customs brokers.
customer: Mid-size EU importers, traders and manufacturers who buy EUDR goods (wood and furniture components, coffee, cocoa, leather, rubber parts, palm derivatives) after a first operator has placed them on the market. The second channel is customs brokers and freight forwarders who white-label the desk.
problem: From 30 Dec 2026, large and medium operators and traders must comply. Downstream operators no longer file due diligence statements but must collect and keep upstream reference and verification numbers for 5 years. They cannot place goods on the market if the numbers are missing when evidently required. One guide estimates 15-30 minutes per supplier per plot for chasing, format fixes and plausibility checks, which is 'several person-weeks' at 150 suppliers, every year. Typical data faults are self-intersecting polygons from phone apps, areas off by 100x, national coordinate systems instead of WGS 84, plots outside the declared country and duplicates.
solution: A forward-to inbox and portal that (1) extracts reference and verification numbers and GeoJSON from supplier emails, PDFs, spreadsheets and invoices; (2) runs geometry checks on closed rings, self-intersection, WGS 84 with six decimals, the 4-hectare polygon rule, plot inside the declared country, duplicates and area versus tonnage plausibility; (3) auto-sends the supplier a plain-language fix request in their language, with a mobile-friendly plot-drawing link; (4) keeps a 5-year evidence vault; and (5) shows a per-purchase-order 'safe to ship or resell' status. Ship a free public GeoJSON validator first as the lead magnet.
why_now: The 30 Dec 2026 application date is fixed. The Commission's May 2026 review said the regulation will not be reopened and proposed a wider product scope through a draft delegated act, so more mid-size buyers will be pulled in. The EU TRACES NT system was reported not fully operational for the December 2025 date, so integration surprises remain.
revenue_model: SaaS tiers of EUR 79-249 per month by supplier count, plus EUR 1-3 per consignment checked. White-label to brokers at EUR 0.50-3 per declaration or a flat EUR 500-2,000 per month. Optional paid supplier-data cleanup projects.
non_obvious_insight: Filing software is crowded, but 'no DDS needed' makes downstream buyers feel safe while they inherit the messiest job: chasing numbers by email from dozens of suppliers, with a 5-year retention duty and a day-one commercial gate. As one guide puts it, 'Market access, not the fine, is the mechanism that will change behaviour first', because customers cannot resell goods without the numbers (https://www.omnia-analytics.at/en/blog/eudr-2026-operator-data-requirements, which also gives the 15-30 minute estimate and the polygon error list). Incorrect polygon format is reported as a leading cause of DDS rejection (https://www.coolset.com/academy/eudr-geolocation-requirements-how-to-collect-and-validate-gps-polygon-data-for-your-dds). Manufacturers 'do not consider themselves agricultural commodity buyers' yet inherit the duty (https://www.regilient.ai/blog/eudr-due-diligence-product-traceability-compliance). Fixing data at the supplier gives free viral distribution, because each supplier serves many buyers.
first_30_days: Build the public GeoJSON checker using open geometry libraries and rank it for searches like 'EUDR GeoJSON self-intersection error'. Pitch 3 customs brokers and 3 coffee, timber or furniture importers with a manual concierge version: they forward supplier emails and you return a cleaned register within 48 hours. Charge EUR 500 for a one-off audit of their existing supplier files. Use the audits to find the 10 most common data faults and build fix templates.

title: Referee Body-Cams and Abuse Evidence Layer
one_liner: A clip-on camera and incident-report service that gives youth and high school officials proof and gives leagues grounds to ban abusive spectators.
customer: State high school associations, officials' associations, youth leagues and tournament operators, paying per official per season.
problem: About 50,000 high school officials have left since 2018, more than 70 percent of new referees quit within three years, and half report feeling unsafe. Insiders assume pay raises fix the shortage, but abuse is the driver and leagues cannot sanction parents or coaches without evidence, so games run short-staffed or get cancelled.
solution: A $50-100 chest-mounted camera or phone clip with audio; speech-to-text flags threats and slurs; league admins get a one-click incident packet (timestamps, transcript, clip) tied to a spectator code of conduct; officials get a private 'safe report' button. Leagues use the evidence to issue bans and support refs.
why_now: 2026 shortage coverage (New York, Utah and others) consistently blames abuse; cheap on-device transcription and body cams make this a $60 problem; national bodies such as USA Volleyball have created formal harassment-response programs, showing appetite.
revenue_model: $40-90 per official per season (hardware included) plus $500-3k per year per league for the admin dashboard; potential insurer partnerships.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is a safety problem, not a pay problem, and the true buyer is the league's risk manager. Recording laws vary by state, so the product is policy-first (posted notices, opt-in associations) and starts where the association mandates it.
first_30_days: Pilot with one regional officials association (about 100 officials) using off-the-shelf action cams and a transcription pipeline, draft a spectator-policy template with a local attorney, run one season of evidence, and convert two leagues into paying customers.

title: Fandom Events in Empty Cinema Auditoriums
one_liner: A rights-plus-ticketing agency that fills weekday auditoriums with VTuber concert viewings, esports finals and game-reveal nights, splitting the box office with cinema chains.
customer: Fandom promoters and community organizers, VTuber agencies, esports and game publishers wanting fan events, and regional cinema chains as venue partners. Fans pay $15-30.
problem: Overseas viewers are about 30% of Hololive viewership and roughly 10B yen of revenue, yet have no communal way to attend, while Sphere-scale venues cost hundreds of millions and Live Nation controls arenas. Independent organizers rent bars with poor AV and no rights.
solution: Package a dark room, great sound and a projection booth with the rest of the event: sublicensed rights, a licensed live feed, all-in-price ticketing, cosplay contests and merch tables. Start with regional independent chains and a fixed menu of event formats.
why_now: Hololive concert revenue grew 18.7% and overseas fandom is underserved. The FTC's all-in-pricing rule and the Live Nation verdict make promoters and fans look for alternatives to arena ticketing. Cinemas still need non-Hollywood content for off-peak seats.
revenue_model: 15-25% of ticket revenue plus $2-8k per event for rights and technical fees, with cinemas taking a box-office split and concessions.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in experience-economy fandom is not a $2B dome, it's a room with audio and projection, which cinemas already own and leave empty midweek. Everyone is chasing IP-in-space capex while the arbitrage is empty seats.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 independent cinema owners on a revenue split. Sign one rights-cleared event, such as a fighting-game grand finals viewing or a licensed VTuber concert screening. Run three test events by day 45 and measure fill rate and concession spend.

title: AV-TEST for Deepfake and Liveness Detectors
one_liner: A buyer-funded independent lab that red-teams deepfake and liveness detectors every month against fresh in-the-wild fakes and publishes procurement-grade scorecards.
customer: Bank and insurer model-risk and fraud-procurement teams, enterprise CISOs buying detection, media organizations, and expert witnesses. All buy annual subscriptions.
problem: Enterprise detection and IDV are the most crowded categories in the brief, and every vendor claims 95-99% accuracy on its own test set. Buyers cannot compare products. Accuracy decays with each new generator, and injection attacks bypass isolated liveness checks. Model-risk officers must validate vendor models but have no independent evidence.
solution: Maintain a continuously refreshed attack corpus: newly released generators, voice clones degraded through phone codecs, virtual-camera and emulator injection, and re-compressed video. Test vendors black-box via API and publish false-accept rates at fixed false-reject rates, cross-generator drift, and time-to-fail after each new model release. Add model-risk documentation packs and court-ready error-rate statements. Vendors may pay only for private testing, never for ranking.
why_now: Detection vendors multiplied in 2025-26 and funding is still flowing (Modulate raised $25M). The injection-attack standard CEN/TS 18099 exists but has almost no commercial third-party lab. The EU AI Act transparency deadline on 2 Dec 2026 and rising fraud losses push buyers to demand proof.
revenue_model: $15-60K per year for full scorecards and monthly refreshes. Custom bake-offs for $25-100K. Expert-witness and litigation support as an upsell.
non_obvious_insight: In the 1990s, antivirus claims were unverifiable until independent labs became the arbiter. Deepfake detection is worse because accuracy decays with every new generator, so buyers need continuous evidence, which is a recurring-revenue product. The real asset is the fresh, hard-to-game attack corpus, and no vendor can build it credibly for itself.
first_30_days: Publish a free baseline report on 10 public detectors using about 300 fresh fakes from the newest open and commercial generators. Send it to 30 bank model-risk leads. Sign 3-5 design-partner subscriptions at about $10K each.

title: Fees-in-Kind: Harvest Becomes School Fee Credit
one_liner: A weigh-in and ledger service that lets parents pay school fees with maize, beans and potatoes at a transparent price, while schools get cheaper, steadier food supply.
customer: Boards of management, principals and bursars of public boarding and day secondary schools, including the new senior-school cohorts, plus rural private schools. The end users are smallholder parents in maize, bean and potato zones.
problem: Farm households are asset-rich and cash-poor exactly when fees fall due in January, May and August. Schools already accept 'a tin of maize' informally, but the value is whatever the storekeeper or bursar decides, with no receipts. Meanwhile the same schools buy food through brokers at inflated tender prices, and government capitation often arrives late. Children still get sent home over arrears even when the parents' store is full of grain. Food is often the largest line in a boarding school's budget.
solution: A Fee Credit Ledger. Farmers deliver graded produce to the school store or a village collection point. A standard weigh ticket (photo of the scale plus a moisture reading) generates an SMS receipt, and the value is credited to the learner's fee account at a published reference price such as NCPB or the county market average, minus a small handling margin. The school gets a weekly reconciliation. On the buying side, the platform, registered as an AGPO-eligible youth or women group (check how each school's procurement committee applies the 30% reservation), bids for school food supply and sources from the same parents. It pools, grades and quality-checks (moisture, aflatoxin spot test). An add-on is hermetic storage bags on credit so parents can deliver later in the term rather than dumping at harvest.
why_now: The first CBC cohort entered senior school in January 2026, expanding boarding and food demand, and the next cohort arrives in January 2027, so schools are planning Term 1 supply now. Capitation delays keep squeezing school food budgets. Cheap Bluetooth scales, moisture meters and M-Pesa and SMS receipts make a trustworthy weigh ticket trivial. Principals in Kenya talk in tight associations, so one working pilot spreads fast.
revenue_model: A 4-8% handling margin on food flow: schools pay below their current broker-inclusive price and farmers receive above the broker price. Later a per-learner per-term ledger fee (about KES 50-100). Once the ledger produces credit-quality data, short-term financing of fee arrears or school receivables.
non_obvious_insight: In every rural ward the school is the largest, most predictable institutional food buyer, and the 'fee arrears list' is a timing and valuation mismatch, not poverty. Fintechs treat barter as embarrassing or informal, but for smallholders paying in maize is the default. What is missing is fair valuation and a ledger everyone trusts. The AGPO set-aside is an under-used entry ticket for farmer groups into school tenders.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 principals through your own old high school or a heads' association branch meeting for a one-term pilot in January 2027. Buy two Bluetooth hanging scales and moisture meters (a few hundred dollars), run the ledger on Google Sheets plus Africa's Talking SMS, and recruit 100 parent households at PTA meetings. Set the price at the midpoint between the farmgate broker price and the school tender price. Register the entity for AGPO and open a supplier profile with the school.

title: Random-Sample CPA Audits of AI Bookkeeping
one_liner: A $79/month independent assurance layer where a licensed CPA reviews a random sample of a micro-business's AI-categorized transactions and signs a monthly accuracy attestation backed by a penalty-reimbursement guarantee.
customer: Nonemployers and 1-10 employee businesses (contractors, salons, restaurants, e-commerce sellers) using AI bookkeeping in QuickBooks, Xero or startup tools. Secondary buyers are AI-bookkeeping vendors wanting white-label certification and lenders wanting attested books.
problem: 46% of AI-using small firms name accuracy as their top problem (Fed SBCS 2026). Intuit and Xero are pushing LLM categorization to millions of users, and Bench's Dec 2024 collapse locked customers out of their books for days. Owners find errors only at a tax bill, a loan denial or a penalty, and new OBBBA reporting (tips and overtime, the $2,000 1099 floor) raises the cost of misclassification.
solution: Stratified sampling weighted toward high-dollar, first-seen-vendor and deduction-sensitive transactions. The CPA confirms against receipts and bank data, fixes errors inside the customer's own software, and issues a monthly signed 'books verified' report with a measured error rate. A small reserve (later insurer-backed) reimburses penalties traceable to verified periods. Every attestation exports to a portable audit file that survives any vendor failing.
why_now: Mass-market LLM bookkeeping arrived in 2026 (Intuit-Anthropic and Xero-Anthropic partnerships) just as CPA headcount stalled near 678K. Intuit cut 17% of staff while opening about 600 offices, which signals that pure-AI trust is unsolved. No incumbent can credibly sell independent assurance on its own output.
revenue_model: $79/month per business with reviewer cost of roughly $15-25/month after AI triage. Add $2-5K/year white-label fees from AI bookkeepers, lender attestation fees, and warranty margin once insurer-backed.
non_obvious_insight: Checking is roughly ten times cheaper than doing, so scarce CPAs can serve 10x more clients as auditors of samples than as preparers. Auditors must be independent of the producer, a position structurally closed to Intuit and Xero. The accumulated error-rate data by tool becomes a Consumer Reports-style asset that the vendors cannot publish themselves.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 part-time or retired CPAs and sign 20 founding clients at $49 from contractor and salon-owner communities. Run a blind test of three AI bookkeepers on 50 anonymized sets of books and publish the error rates for press. Pitch 3 small bookkeeping firms to resell the attestation.

title: GLP-1 Stipend-in-a-Box for Small Employers
one_liner: A counsel-reviewed HRA wrapper that lets small employers subsidize $149-$299 cash-pay GLP-1s with a capped monthly stipend.
customer: Employers with roughly 10-200 employees, sold through brokers, PEOs and HRA administrators.
problem: Large-employer coverage fell from 72% to 60% and more are dropping, while 27% of employers already point staff to LillyDirect or NovoCare. Direct-to-employer vendors like Waltz Health and 9amHealth target mid and large plans. Small employers can't carve out of a fully insured plan, and stipend plans raise ERISA, ACA and tax questions they can't answer.
solution: A packaged structure (QSEHRA, ICHRA or limited-purpose HRA, depending on group size) with plan documents, capped stipend rules, receipt-based reimbursement from DTC pharmacies, minimum-essential-coverage checks, and optional coaching. Brokers get a commission.
why_now: $149-$299 manufacturer cash prices make a capped stipend cheaper than open-ended coverage. Employers just dropped or plan to drop coverage before open enrollment, and TrumpRx and DTC channels launched in 2026.
revenue_model: $5-8 per employee per month plus ~5% of stipend flow, with broker commission share.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is over who administers the wrapper for the 90% of employers that PBM carve-out vendors don't serve. Compliance and broker distribution matter more than the coaching content.
first_30_days: Have an ERISA attorney draft the plan documents. Partner with an existing QSEHRA or HRA administrator. Pilot with 10 small employers (~300 lives) through two brokers and measure uptake and cost per participant.

title: Continuity Retainer for One-Licensee Funeral Homes
one_liner: Key-person insurance for funeral homes: a bench of pre-credentialed licensed directors and embalmers who step in within 24-48 hours when the owner is sick, burned out or gone, with a built-in path to succession.
customer: Independent and rural funeral homes with one or two licensed staff (roughly 30-150 calls a year), typically owner-operators aged 55-75. A second buyer is the family of an owner who has died or fallen ill and needs the home kept legal while it is sold.
problem: States require a licensed funeral director or manager-in-charge, and often a licensed embalmer, for an establishment to operate. The owner is on call 24/7/365 and hasn't had a real week off in years. One heart attack, surgery or burnout means the home cannot legally operate, families get funneled to the consolidator down the road, and a business built over three generations is sold at a distressed price. Informal 'relief director' phone lists exist, but there is no bench, no contract, no reciprocity or board paperwork handled, and no guarantee anyone answers at 3 a.m.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired licensed directors and embalmers, including many leaving consolidators, and pre-credential them in a target state cluster with background checks and reciprocity filings. Sell continuity retainers that guarantee a set number of coverage days a year (real vacations, weekends off) plus emergency activation within 24-48 hours at a day rate. The company handles the state-board notice of interim manager changes. A succession track lets an interim operator or next-generation licensed buyer convert into a partner or buyer with seller financing, so owners have an alternative to a roll-up.
why_now: Consolidation keeps shrinking the independent pool (SCI alone bought about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025). The licensed workforce is aging while mortuary-school pipelines are thin. Rising cremation lowers revenue per case, making full-time second hires unaffordable for small homes. Rural closures are creating 'funeral deserts'. Many states have passed occupational-license recognition laws that make multi-state relief staffing easier.
revenue_model: Retainer of $900-$2,000/month per home including N coverage days. Activation day rate of $800-$1,400 billed to the home, with a 25-30% margin over what the licensee is paid. Per-case fees for trade embalming and prep-room services. A 1-2% success fee on succession transactions.
non_obvious_insight: The real asset of an independent funeral home isn't the building, it's one license holder with a phone, and that is a single point of failure. Consolidators know it and wait. Owners will pay to sleep: this is a wellness and continuity product disguised as staffing, and its best feature is the succession pipeline it creates once a trusted operator is already inside the home.
first_30_days: Recruit eight retired licensed directors and embalmers through state association chapters and retiree groups. Check each state board's rules for temporary manager-in-charge designation. Pitch 20 one-licensee homes in two adjacent counties at a $1,200/month founding rate with a 'test weekend off' guarantee. Sign the first three, and run the first covered weekend within 30 days to produce a testimonial.

title: IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents
one_liner: Rich parents win school disputes with a paid educational advocate and paper trail; for $20/mo, give parents of the roughly 7.5M US students with IEPs a chief of staff who watches the legal clocks and logs every missed service minute.
customer: Parents of children with IEPs (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language delay), sold through state and local special-ed parent groups, parent training centers, pediatric practices, disability law clinics and credit unions.
problem: Districts arrive with a team; wealthy families bring an advocate ($150-400/hr) and an attorney. Federal enforcement was hollowed out (mass OSEP layoffs in October 2025, and reported moves of oversight to HHS and civil-rights enforcement to DOJ in June 2026), so parents are effectively on their own. Most violations are procedural (late evaluations, missing prior written notice, services not delivered) and go unnoticed because nobody keeps the clocks.
solution: Parent uploads the IEP and evaluations. The system builds the legal calendar (evaluation timelines from consent, meeting-notice windows, annual and triennial reviews, progress-report cadence), drafts records requests, creates a one-page pre-meeting brief (top asks plus data), and sends a same-day 'memorializing' follow-up email with prior-written-notice requests after meetings. It logs service minutes delivered vs promised, quantifying missed minutes for a compensatory-services claim, and scans the IEP for defects (no baselines, unmeasurable goals). Advocates are on-demand at $75 per 30 minutes, with a path to state complaint and due process.
why_now: The federal special-ed enforcement vacuum is documented and new as of late 2025 and mid-2026. IEP counts are rising, and LLMs can parse messy IEP PDFs and draft procedurally precise letters. Parent communities are organized on Facebook and Reddit and actively looking for help.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $75 advocate sessions with a revenue split to a vetted advocate co-op; $3-6 per member per month from parent centers, pediatric groups and credit unions; district-facing analytics sold only with parent consent, later.
non_obvious_insight: What the rich buy is not better argument but continuous procedural pressure: dated, written, specific requests. The subscription funds clock-watching and documentation, not advice. Parents who log service minutes turn 'I feel they're not delivering' into a quantified claim, and the paper trail is the evidence in any later dispute, so value compounds over time.
first_30_days: Publish a free IEP clock calculator and letter templates. Partner with admins of 10 state-level special-ed Facebook groups and concierge 30 families manually, measuring violations found. Convert those families to $20/mo and recruit 5 advocates for the on-demand tier.

title: Cross-Lab Calibration Plates for AI Training Data
one_liner: Ready-to-run reference plates and normalization software that make data from different labs, robots and cloud labs comparable enough to train models on.
customer: AI drug-discovery companies that merge internal, CRO and cloud-lab data, high-content screening groups, and cloud labs and CROs that want certified comparability.
problem: Trend chain: autonomous labs, cloud labs and philanthropic data programs multiply data streams. Models then cannot separate batch from biology. The JUMP Cell Painting consortium needed a 302-compound positive-control plate on every batch across 13 sites, and a cross-site organoid study found 2,188 differentially expressed genes by day 84. Physical reference standards for functional assays are not commercially supplied.
solution: Ship 'Reference Plate v1': lot-certified frozen reference cells (a defined iPSC-derived line at a fixed passage), the open JUMP-Target compound set, spike-ins and controls, all pre-plated. Customers run it on every batch. SaaS returns per-plate correction vectors, drift alarms and a 'harmonized to Reference v1' certificate. Expand to viability, high-content imaging and scRNA-seq perturbation assays.
why_now: Lila, Medra, Transfyr and other autonomous-lab efforts are producing data at scale. The OpenAI Foundation's $1B Public Data for Health grants will fund data generation whose cross-site comparability nobody audits. Batch-correction methods are mature, but no shared physical standard exists.
revenue_model: $250-600 per plate, $2-6k/month software, and $10-30k certification audits for labs and CROs.
non_obvious_insight: ERCC spike-ins and NIST-style standards made genomics data poolable. Functional assays lack an equivalent. Standards are winner-take-most: the first plate adopted by three or four major datasets becomes the de facto unit. Physical lots are also a moat that software-only AI shops cannot copy.
first_30_days: Source the JUMP-Target compound set. Produce 200 pilot plates. Give them free to 5 AI startups and cloud labs for a cross-site comparison. Publish the batch-variance reduction and convert the users to paid.

title: Chargeback Guarantee for Agent-Placed Orders
one_liner: A merchant-side gateway that checks the shopper's signed mandate against the cart, keeps a tamper-proof decision record, and reimburses chargebacks on approved agent orders.
customer: Shopify, BigCommerce and headless merchants doing $5M-$100M GMV that have switched on agentic checkout (ACP, UCP, AP2) and whose acquirers watch their dispute ratios.
problem: Fraud engines score human signals (device, mouse, session) that agents lack, so agent orders are either falsely declined or approved blind. Disputes have no rulebook: neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding chargeback rule for agent-initiated purchases, the record shows only merchant, timestamp and amount, and Visa's dispute threshold tightened from 2.2% to 1.5% on 2026-04-01. Merchants also have to support ACP, UCP, AP2, MPP and x402 separately.
solution: One integration that accepts all five protocols. It cryptographically verifies the user-signed mandate (spend cap, item constraints, expiry, agent identity) against what was actually ordered, stores an immutable decision record, and auto-builds representment packets. Orders that pass are guaranteed: we pay the chargeback and the fee. Underwriting rests on mandate-versus-cart match, not on behavioral fingerprinting.
why_now: The protocols went live in the last 8 months (MPP 2026-03-18, plus ACP, UCP, AP2, TAP, Verifiable Intent). Agent usage is about 62% at comparison but only about 23% at checkout, so trust is the bottleneck. The Ninth Circuit's 2026-08-04 Comet ruling treats the agent as the user, and there is still no fault rulebook from the networks.
revenue_model: 0.5-1.0% of guaranteed agent-order GMV plus $299-1,999 per month gateway SaaS. The guarantee reserve is backed by a $1-2M capital line or a quota-share reinsurer. Loss data can later be licensed to insurers and networks.
non_obvious_insight: Incumbent fraud models are trained on human behavior, so agent traffic is behaviorally blank. The right signal is the mandate, not the session. Whoever holds the mandate-versus-cart record and the loss outcomes becomes the arbiter that networks, acquirers and insurers will need, and that same data is the missing underwriting telemetry for agent risk generally. Merchants will not want to pick among five protocols, so the guarantee is the wedge for owning the plumbing.
first_30_days: Ship a Shopify app in shadow mode for 15-20 merchants: tag agent-origin orders (agent referrers, ACP/UCP headers), log mandates, and back-test which orders would have been disputed. Offer the first 5 merchants a 90-day guarantee capped at $50k each, funded by founder capital plus a small MGA or reinsurer line, at about 0.75% of agent GMV. Publish the observed dispute rates as the pricing basis.

title: Pay-on-Green: Escrow Released by Executable Tests
one_liner: Escrow for agent-to-agent work where the negotiated object is a hashed acceptance test, and money moves only when the test passes.
customer: Growth, data and ops teams at 20-500 person companies that subcontract bulk deliverables (data enrichment, scraping, code migrations, translation with QA) to other vendors' agents, plus the small agent vendors who want guaranteed payment.
problem: Card chargebacks do not fit machine-speed commerce and stablecoin payments are irreversible. The dispute in agent work is almost always 'was it good enough?', and no human can review thousands of small deliverables. The 2026 payment protocols (AP2, ACP, x402, MPP) settle payment but say little about quality or delayed fulfilment.
solution: A 'test-as-contract' escrow. Before work starts, buyer and seller agents agree on an executable acceptance suite: schema and checksum checks, unit tests, planted canary items with known answers, and a rubric graded by a panel of three different-model judges with pre-committed prompts. Funds lock in escrow. On delivery the suite runs in a sandbox and releases funds item by item (partial settlement). Disputes narrow to 'was the test fair?' and go to a small-claims panel with human appeal. Third parties publish reusable verifier suites and earn a royalty per run.
why_now: Agents in 2026 routinely delegate subtasks to other vendors' agents. LLM-as-judge and cheap sandboxes are mature. Four competing payment protocols now exist, and academic proposals for refundable, delayed-fulfilment settlement (for example the Agentic Settlement Protocol paper of September 2026) show the dispute layer is an acknowledged gap.
revenue_model: 1.5-3% escrow fee on GMV, plus $0.01-0.05 per verifier run, plus a royalty share to verifier authors. Enterprise plan with SLAs and private test libraries.
non_obvious_insight: Move the dispute before the money moves. Agents will not argue price, they will argue the test, so the durable asset is a growing library of standard acceptance suites, which works like an ISO standard for agent deliverables. Planted canaries (honeypot items, as crowdsourcing platforms use) catch lazy or fraudulent sellers cheaply.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical where canaries are easy: bulk lead-list verification and web-data extraction. Recruit 5 small agent vendors and 3 buyers from indie-hacker and MCP developer communities. Run escrow manually on Stripe Connect with delayed payouts. Publish 20 open-source acceptance-test templates as lead magnets. Charge 3% and aim for $10k of escrowed GMV.

title: Screw-Pile Foundations That Skip the Concrete Crew
one_liner: Engineered helical-pile foundations with torque-logged QA and prefab floor cassettes, installed in a day, for spec homes, ADUs and factory-built homes where foundation crews are booked out for weeks.
customer: Spec and production builders in crew-constrained markets (Texas, Florida), ADU builders and factory-built home dealers.
problem: Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and loan interest keeps accruing while 15-20 houses wait 6+ weeks. Forming, pouring and finishing are crew-dependent and hard to automate. Chassis-free factory homes need light foundations that are quick to install.
solution: A foundation-only subcontractor installing helical piles with a torque-monitoring logger and structural details pre-approved by a partner engineer for three soil regions, plus a prefab insulated floor cassette or steel grade beam. Torque logs become an objective, timestamped QA report for inspectors and lenders. Autonomous pile driving, already proven in solar, is the roadmap.
why_now: Enforcement and labor shortages are stretching foundation crews. Autonomous pile-driving rigs are commercial in solar. Chassis-free homes and the ADU boom create demand for light foundations. Lenders and inspectors increasingly accept digital QA data.
revenue_model: Priced roughly at parity with slab or stem-wall per home and sold on speed, with margin from utilization. Per-sq-ft or per-home pricing, plus licensing engineered details to other installers.
non_obvious_insight: Changing the design removes the scarce trade from the critical path entirely. Insiders try to hire or automate concrete crews, but a foundation with no forms, no cure time and no finishers becomes a machine-and-engineering task with objective logs.
first_30_days: Engage a geotech and a structural PE for standard details. Rent a mini-excavator with a torque head. Sign two builders with stuck lots or ADUs, install three foundations, and document schedule savings versus their alternatives.

title: Delivery Robots for Gated Communities
one_liner: Buy the sidewalk-robot fleets that failed on public streets at a discount and run them inside senior-living, campus and large apartment communities as a subscription amenity.
customer: Operators of senior-living and continuing-care communities, hospital campuses, student housing, military bases and large HOAs. They pay a monthly amenity fee.
problem: Sidewalk delivery fails on demand density, not on technology. Serve built about 2,000 robots but booked $2.65M of 2025 revenue, roughly $1.3k per robot by my arithmetic. Meanwhile private communities are labor-squeezed and struggle to get meals, pharmacy items and packages to residents.
solution: Closed-loop robots on private paths deliver dining-hall meals, pharmacy pickups, mail and supplies within one campus. Use secondhand hardware, a light fleet-management layer, and teleop backup for edge cases. Price as a fixed monthly amenity fee plus a small per-delivery charge.
why_now: Sidewalk-delivery unit economics visibly broke in 2025-26, so hardware is cheap and experienced operators are available. Vision-language navigation cuts per-site mapping cost, and last-mile contractors are closing (4XH and Ardor), which shows how expensive human delivery labor has become.
revenue_model: $3-8k a month per community platform fee, plus $1-2 per delivery. Hardware is bundled or financed. Target 8-12 robots per community at about 60% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: A subscription amenity decouples revenue from order volume, which is exactly what killed the public-street model. A private campus also removes the permit, ADA and pedestrian-liability problems and guarantees density.
first_30_days: Pick 3 continuing-care or student-housing campuses in one metro. Buy or lease 3-5 used robots from a fleet operator raising cash. Run a teleop-assisted pilot delivering meals to about 20 residents, and convert one campus to a signed LOI at about $4k a month.

title: CMMC Enclave for CNC Shops
one_liner: A prebuilt, shop-floor-aware CUI enclave and evidence pack that gets 20-person machine shops through CMMC Level 2 without rebuilding their IT.
customer: Job shops and small manufacturers making parts for defense primes (castings, forgings, machined parts), roughly 30,000-plus firms in the defense supply base.
problem: CMMC Level 2 assessments for contract awards ramp up from Nov 2026 (verify dates). Shops keep CUI drawings on machine-side PCs and USB sticks, and generic CMMC consultants scope the entire company. Sub-tier suppliers lack IT staff and capital, exactly the bottleneck AIA-Bain describes.
solution: A managed enclave that isolates only the CAD/CAM and CNC controllers handling CUI, ships as a pre-configured appliance plus cloud tenant, and comes with policies, evidence collection and assessor liaison. Fixed monthly price, no consultants hourly.
why_now: Phase-in of the CMMC rule puts assessment on contracts through 2026-27, and primes are pushing flow-down requirements. Sub-tier financing is scarce, so shops need a low-capex option.
revenue_model: $800-2,500 per month per shop plus $5-15K onboarding. Channel through primes who will subsidize their suppliers' compliance.
non_obvious_insight: Scope reduction is the whole business. The winning product understands machine tool OT and draws a tight boundary around it, while horizontal CMMC vendors sell a heavy enterprise program.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 shops through a regional manufacturing extension partnership. Assemble the appliance from commodity parts. Sign one prime's supplier program as channel.

title: Half-Plate Menus for GLP-1 Diners
one_liner: A menu-engineering and POS program that turns GLP-1 diners into incremental visits through protein-first half portions.
customer: Multi-unit casual-dining and fast-casual operators with 20-300 locations.
problem: GLP-1 households cut restaurant spend about 8%, yet 48% of users say they would dine out more if smaller portions were offered.
solution: Design a 'Half-Plate' section (65-70% of full price, protein-forward, fiber-tuned), integrate it in the POS, and measure incremental visits and margin per cover.
why_now: About 12% of Americans use a GLP-1 and the oral Wegovy pill launched in January 2026 at $149-299/month, so the segment is now big enough for a dedicated menu line.
revenue_model: Per-location monthly fee plus a performance share of measured incremental visits.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume smaller portions cannibalize revenue, but restaurant labor and rent are per-cover costs. A visit at 70% of the check with lower food cost beats losing the visit at 100%.
first_30_days: Sign two regional chains for a 10-store test of a Half-Plate section and set up a simple visit-frequency and basket dashboard from POS exports.

title: Loss-Curve Intelligence for Autonomous Trucking Insurance
one_liner: A benchmark and risk-scoring workbench that helps insurers, brokers and carriers price driverless-truck coverage using evidence instead of 'unknown'.
customer: Specialty insurers and reinsurers, MGAs, brokers, and large trucking carriers. AV operators such as Aurora, Kodiak, Bot Auto and Gatik also buy, to lower their premiums.
problem: Insurers price AV trucks 'slightly above' human drivers purely because of the unknown, with premiums expected to fall 15-25% a year. Werner's CIO says 'we have a gap' on pricing. Nobody has normalized exposure data by operating domain.
solution: Ingest public crash reports (NHTSA Standing General Order and state reports), published safety cases and operator-contributed telemetry. Build frequency and severity priors by operating design domain (lane type, speed, weather, time of day) and deliver a quarterly benchmark plus a route and lane risk-scoring API. Later, underwrite as an MGA.
why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and 500k+ driverless miles, the first real exposure data, and targets 30,000 trucks by 2030. Insurers must reprice yearly and need evidence to justify each step down.
revenue_model: $75-250k a year in subscriptions from insurers and reinsurers, per-policy data fees, and MGA commission (10-15% of premium) once loss data supports it.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not too few miles but the lack of a standard exposure unit. Whoever defines miles by operating domain as the accepted denominator becomes the FICO of autonomy, and operators will share data because it lowers their premiums.
first_30_days: Build an ODD-normalized frequency table from public NHTSA data. Interview 15 trucking and AV underwriters, send a free 'AV vs human benchmark' brief to 3 brokers, and close one $30k paid pilot with an MGA.

title: Men's Repair Crews Funded by Aging-in-Place Budgets
one_liner: A membership club for men 25-45 who show up weekly to do minor home repairs for isolated older adults, led by a paid tradesperson and paid for by aging-in-place budgets.
customer: Payers are Medicare Advantage plans (home-safety supplemental benefits), Area Agencies on Aging, city aging-in-place funds and Medicaid home-modification programs, paying $400-900 per job. Members add about $30 a month in dues.
problem: Men reject talk-based loneliness solutions, and therapy framing fails them. Men's Sheds show that shoulder-to-shoulder tasks build belonging (97% of members in one survey said they have a place where they belong), but they run on charity money. Meanwhile older adults with unfixed stairs, missing grab bars and poor lighting fall, and licensed repair labor for small jobs is scarce and expensive.
solution: Crews of 8-10 men with one paid licensed lead. A 3-hour Saturday job (grab bars, rails, ramps, lighting, smoke alarms) followed by a shared meal. Rotating pairs do check-in visits. Software handles referral intake from care managers, photo scoping, materials, volunteer liability coverage, and payer invoicing with before/after proof and a fall-risk checklist.
why_now: Male loneliness is now a headline metric (WHO commission, Jun 2025) but products remain talk-based. Medicare Advantage plans are under margin pressure and favor cheap benefits with hard outcomes such as fall prevention. Programs modeled on CAPABLE (repairs plus clinician visits) have shown large drops in daily-living disability. Trades labor is short.
revenue_model: Per-job fees from payers ($400-900), member dues, and materials sponsorship from hardware retailers. Volunteer labor makes the gross margin work. Later: employer-sponsored membership.
non_obvious_insight: Men join for a task, not a talk, so give them a task that a payer already funds and cannot staff. The 'male loneliness' problem and the 'home-modification labor shortage' are the same market seen from two sides.
first_30_days: Partner with one Area Agency on Aging or a Rebuilding Together affiliate that already has a waitlist of households. Recruit 8 men via a local run club, climbing gym and Reddit. Hire a retired contractor as lead at about $40 an hour. Complete 4 pilot jobs at $350 each, document outcomes, and pitch two Medicare Advantage care-management teams with the first 20 jobs.

title: Recorded Parent Voices, Endowed to Outlive Us
one_liner: Guided, human-only voice and video milestone messages for the children of dying parents, with the hosting prepaid so the recordings outlive the company.
customer: Terminally ill parents of minor children, or their spouses. Referrals come from oncology and young-adult cancer social workers, child-life specialists, and hospice social workers. Hospice foundations sponsor families who cannot pay.
problem: Dying parents of young children want to leave their actual voice for the 16th birthday, the wedding and the first heartbreak. They start too late. By the time hospice admission happens, many patients are too sedated, breathless or confused to record anything usable. The generic tools (StoryWorth-style prompts, phone voice memos) produce rambling, prompt-less files. Families also do not trust vendors to still exist in 20 years. Meanwhile AI voice-cloning 'deadbots' are being pitched at the same families, and most of them recoil.
solution: A two-session guided capture (in person or on video) run by a trained 'legacy guide' with a chaplain or child-bereavement background. It uses a prompt library organized by the child's future age: what a 12-year-old needs to hear versus a 30-year-old. Examples: 'how I met your dad', 'what I was afraid of', 'what I'd say when you're furious at me', and a mundane category (how I laughed, my opinion of your first crush) that grown children say matters most. The output is edited, human-only audio and video with a strict no-synthesis policy. Each message is tagged to a milestone and delivered by the surviving guardian's app. There is a physical archival copy and printed transcripts. Hosting is prepaid into a trust-held reserve, with a contractual right to export everything if the company dies. Durability and authenticity are the product, not features.
why_now: AI voice-cloning is now cheap and good enough that grief-tech is being flooded with synthetic 'talk to your dead mom' products. Public and clinical unease about them is rising, which opens a clear 'only what they actually said' position. At least some early digital-afterlife vendors have folded or pivoted, so buyers are primed to ask 'will this exist in 2045?'. Phone-quality recording is now good enough that no studio is needed. I could not verify specific vendor failures in this session, so confirm before using them in marketing.
revenue_model: Roughly $450 for guided capture plus a one-time $600 to $900 permanence endowment (about $1,000 to $1,400 per family). The endowment funds 30-year hosting, and the reserve is held in a trust or escrow. Add-ons: printed keepsake book, extra milestone messages, and an 'audio blessing' set for each child. Hospice and hospital foundations sponsor uninsured families at a discounted wholesale rate.
non_obvious_insight: The market timing is wrong in everyone's mind. The recording window closes weeks before hospice, so the referral source is oncology, not hospice. What dying parents fear most is not death but vanishing, and that includes the file vanishing. Buyers will pay more for a credible 'this outlives our company' promise than for any feature. Refusing to synthesize is a selling point that families and chaplains will repeat.
first_30_days: Recruit two oncology or child-life social workers as design partners. Run 8 to 10 free pilot sessions using a phone and a $60 lavalier mic, and write the age-banded prompt library from what the kids' guardians say they'd want. Get a small-estates attorney or trust company to set up the escrow and export-if-we-fail clause. Put up a one-page site, then charge from case 11. Ask the first families for a written testimonial and referrals to two other oncology units.

title: Second-Look Verification for Imagery-Based Nonrenewals
one_liner: A $50-80, 48-hour human check between an aerial-imagery flag and a nonrenewal, sold to carriers' compliance teams.
customer: Regional and mid-size homeowners carriers and MGAs in California, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and New York, bought by underwriting and compliance leads.
problem: Imagery-driven nonrenewals are generating regulatory heat (a Florida owner with 52 claim-free years was dropped with no inspection). California AB 75 became operative July 1 2026, requiring notice, a copy of the photos, a dispute path and a remediation window. CT, NH and PA regulators say imagery alone is insufficient, and a NY bill is pending. In-person inspections cost far more and take weeks.
solution: A guided homeowner video capture with fraud checks, or a local gig inspector, returning structured findings mapped to the carrier's rules. It auto-generates the compliant notice package and remediation checklist, and keeps an audit log for regulators.
why_now: AB 75 took effect July 1 2026, and other states are moving.
revenue_model: Per flagged policy plus a platform fee.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators demand more than imagery, but nobody wants $250 inspections. The lower price point makes compliance affordable at scale and sells to a budget-holding compliance team.
first_30_days: Call 10 regional carriers' compliance heads and pilot with 200 flagged policies. Prove the share of imagery flags that human review clears.

title: Cool-Cap Ledger: Indoor Temperature Evidence for Landlords
one_liner: Low-cost sensors and tamper-evident logs that give landlords, tenants and inspectors one accepted reading of indoor temperature.
customer: Owners and property managers of 10+ unit buildings in Maryland (80F cap since June 1 2026), LA County (82F from Jan 1 2027) and NYC (78F cap, owner duty from 2030). Tenant groups and code enforcement are secondary buyers.
problem: Cooling caps are enforced by complaint, so the fight will be over readings: a tenant's phone app against a landlord with no record. Landlords face fines and habitability suits with no defensible data, and tenants cannot prove violations.
solution: $30 sensors in a sampled set of units, third-party-verifiable logs, a tenant-visible dashboard, automated compliance reports and a dispute-response pack. An upsell is a unit-level cooling-gap map for capex planning, showing which units to retrofit first under LA County's phase-in.
why_now: Maryland's cap is already live, LA County starts in about 3 months, and NYC Local Law 2026/023 is passed. The summer 2026 heat set off a wave of complaints.
revenue_model: $4-8 per unit per month for landlords, plus municipal enforcement licenses.
non_obvious_insight: In a complaint-driven regime, evidence is the product. Neutral data protects landlords from false claims and tenants from real violations, so both sides will accept it.
first_30_days: Sign 5-10 LA County and Maryland property managers for winter pilots ahead of the Jan 2027 start. Build the logging and report pack, and pilot in 100 units.

title: Cross-Landlord Fake-Employer and Fake-Reference Registry
one_liner: A shared network that spots rental fraud by the out-of-band details forgers cannot fake, such as the same 'HR' phone number, burner line or 'previous landlord' reused across dozens of leasing offices.
customer: Independent and mid-size property managers (50 to 5,000 units) who process applications themselves and lack a fraud team. They pay per application or per portfolio. Later customers are auto lenders, buy-here-pay-here dealers, gig-work platforms and small-balance mortgage lenders, who all verify employers and references the same way.
problem: Application fraud is now professional. The pay stubs, bank statements and offer letters are fabricated, and the 'employer' is a shell whose 'HR line' is answered by an accomplice. Even the 'previous landlord' reference is a friend. Every leasing office catches one of these files, throws it out, and never tells anyone. The same ring then applies at the property across town and eventually gets a lease. The eviction that follows costs $8,000 to $20,000 and several months. Document-forensics tools catch sloppy Photoshop, but once image generators can produce perfect pay stubs (as they now can), the lie is no longer in the PDF. It is in the phone number and the employer that do not exist.
solution: An API and browser extension for leasing staff. Staff enter the employer name, HR phone or email, the previous-landlord contact and the stated address. The system returns a risk read built from three signals. First, telecom line-type and age (VoIP or burner, number recently ported or activated). Second, business-registry and domain checks (EIN, formation date, mismatched address, brand-new domain). Third, and this is the moat, network signals: how many distinct applicants at how many unrelated landlords used this exact phone, email, employer or landlord reference in the last 12 months, and whether any of those files were confirmed fraud by a participating PM. Participants contribute confirmed-fraud entities and get read access, and entries link to entities (phones, domains, businesses), not to named individuals. That design keeps most of the data outside consumer-report regulation, and any person-linked entry gets a dispute and correction workflow.
why_now: Generative image models make forged financial documents indistinguishable in 2025 and 2026, which pushes the defensive signal from document pixels to out-of-band verification. Fraud-detection vendors for leasing are consolidating around documents, so an entity-level shared registry sits in the gap. Large PMs have internal fraud teams, and the long tail of independents has nothing. Rental markets that are softer with more concessions also attract more fraud-ring activity aimed at free-rent giveaways and quick move-ins.
revenue_model: $1.50 to $3.00 per application check, or $149 to $499 per month by portfolio size with a contribution-based discount. Enterprise API licensing to lenders and platforms later. Data-contribution credits make the network self-seeding.
non_obvious_insight: Rental fraud rings reuse infrastructure across landlords far more than they reuse identities. The same 'HR' number answers for 14 different companies. But no single landlord sees more than one or two, so the pattern is invisible without a network. It works like ISO ClaimSearch did for insurance claims. Because the registry tracks entities and not people, it sidesteps most of the fair-lending and consumer-reporting objections that killed earlier landlord blacklists.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 PMs from local NARPM chapters and landlord Facebook groups. Ask each to send the last 20 to 50 confirmed-fraud files (phone, email, employer, reference only, no SSNs), and seed the database from those. Run the pooled data for overlaps and show each PM how many of their 'unique' fraudsters overlapped with someone else's. Ship a Chrome extension that checks a phone or email against the database plus Twilio Lookup. Free for the first 60 days for contributors, then $149 per month. Have a fair-credit-reporting attorney review the entity-only design and the dispute process before charging.

title: TurkBridge: MTurk-Compatible Verified-Human Marketplace
one_liner: An MTurk requester-API-compatible endpoint backed by an identity-verified, proof-of-human worker pool, launched as Amazon Mechanical Turk closes on 30 Sept 2026.
customer: Academic labs and survey researchers, small ML data-labeling teams, and apps that use human-in-the-loop micro-tasks through boto3 or psiTurk-style code. Displaced MTurk workers are the supply side.
problem: Amazon closes MTurk on 30 Sept 2026 and the FAQ names no alternatives or migration path. New HITs end 30 Sept, bonuses are possible until 30 Oct, and transaction history is inaccessible after 28 Jan 2027. SageMaker Ground Truth and Augmented AI lose the MTurk worker type on the same date. Requesters have legacy code and no drop-in replacement, and quality was already collapsing because workers submitted AI output. One HN user says their app 'has been using Amazon Mechanical Turk for left-pad queries, and that service is shutting down in less than two weeks.'
solution: (1) Publish an API shim that mimics the MTurk requester operations (CreateHIT, ListAssignmentsForHIT, ApproveAssignment, qualification requirements, sandbox), so a codebase migrates by changing an endpoint URL. (2) Build supply from ex-MTurk workers on Turkopticon and worker forums, who lose income on the closure date. Give each worker a verified unique-person identity, passkey and liveness checks, and behavioural anti-LLM signals. (3) Sell two tiers, 'verified human' and 'domain expert', with paid-per-task quality gates. The product is the proof that a human did the work, priced above the old race-to-the-bottom rate.
why_now: The shutdown date is two days away, and worker income disappears the same day. Generic open crowd platforms have been wrecked by LLMs, so verified humanness has become the scarce good. Identity-verification APIs are now cheap (Didit, 'Stripe for Identity Verification', launched on HN in March 2026).
revenue_model: A 20-30% take on task payments, a $99/mo lab plan with participant-screening tools, and a per-verification fee for enterprise annotation buyers.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is trust in who is doing the task, and the API compatibility is what lets you take the customers. The MTurk FAQ confirms the dates and lists no alternative or migration path (https://www.mturk.com/help). In the 534-point HN thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49457545), dubeye writes: 'The problem as I see it is verifying the work is not done by AI. If it was possible to verify somehow that the work is definitely not done by AI I think there would still be a market.' Another user found MNIST accuracy from Ground Truth on MTurk 'marginally better than guessing.' Prolific is named as the maintained alternative, but I found no evidence that any alternative offers MTurk API compatibility. Legacy scripts are the switching cost, and the shim removes it.
first_30_days: Week 1: write the shim covering the 6 most-used MTurk operations, using boto3's endpoint_url override. Post a 'migrate in 10 minutes' guide on r/mturk, psiTurk and academic Twitter. Weeks 2-3: onboard the first 300-500 workers with ID and liveness checks. Recruit 5 lab requesters with free credits in exchange for case studies. Week 4: run paid studies, publish a proof-of-human quality comparison against raw MTurk data, and start charging the take rate.

title: Independent Safety Registry for Pet Medicines
one_liner: A neutral post-market surveillance system for veterinary drugs and biologics, built on pet-insurance claims plus owner-reported outcomes.
customer: Animal-health drugmakers and biologics developers (safety and medical-affairs teams) pay subscriptions. Pet insurers and MGAs pay for cost-effectiveness analytics. Vet groups and foundations use the public lookup.
problem: Vet adverse-event reporting is voluntary and underreported, and after the 2025 controversy over reported adverse events with anti-NGF antibody injections for canine osteoarthritis, owners and vets have no independent way to weigh safety signals. Pharma-run surveillance is not trusted. Insurers hold the only longitudinal cross-clinic data, yet are pushing 19.7% premium increases on 9% more animals without knowing which treatments reduce downstream claims. New modalities (mAbs, CGMs, long-acting insulins, oral oncology, and possibly a canine longevity drug) are arriving with no owner for outcomes data.
solution: A data trust that ingests de-identified claims from partner insurers and MGAs, optional practice-management extracts, and owner-reported outcomes gathered by a QR code at the clinic. It runs disproportionality signal detection in the style of FDA Sentinel. Outputs are (a) a safety dashboard for drug makers, (b) formulary and cost-effectiveness reports for insurers, and (c) a public 'what happened to dogs like mine' lookup for vets and owners.
why_now: Premiums rose 19.7% against 9% more animals, so insurers need loss-control insight. Big biologics and Loyal's longevity program (1,317 dogs in the STAY study, FDA acceptance of efficacy and safety sections) mean a wave of new launches. IDEXX buying CoVet shows workflow data is becoming a strategic asset, and independent players need a neutral alternative.
revenue_model: Pharma subscriptions of $60-250k per product family per year. Insurer analytics contracts of $50-150k per year. Custom post-marketing studies at $100-300k. A free public tier drives owner-reported data.
non_obvious_insight: Companion-animal medicine is the last big therapeutic area with no Sentinel-style system, and insurers are the only long-lived holders of cross-clinic data. After a public safety scare, drugmakers will pay for credibility that they cannot generate themselves, and insurers will pay for the same data to reduce claims.
first_30_days: Pitch small MGAs and startup insurers (hungry for analytics, less locked into data rules) on a free pilot in exchange for a data-sharing agreement. Build signal detection for the 10 most common drugs and biologics. Publish a public report on one hot topic, then sell two pharma safety leads a pilot subscription. Expect first revenue at month 4-6.
